    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause.
    • We are seeking a detail-oriented QA Specialist to ensure that every email and SMS campaign and journey is configured correctly and functions as intended prior to launch.
    • Conduct QA on all email and SMS campaigns and journeys in Iterable prior to launch to ensure every element is configured correctly and functions as intended.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause. We’ve built all of our technology in-house including an EHR, patient care admin system, patient portal, website, marketing technology etc. Winona has two compounding pharmacies and a team of in-house physicians providing world-class care via a fully vertically integrated business model.

    We are seeking a detail-oriented QA Specialist to ensure that every email and SMS campaign and journey is configured correctly and functions as intended prior to launch. This role spans campaign configuration and tracking, content and design review, and cross-platform QA — identifying and resolving concerns before they reach our audience.

    Seniority Level: Junior–Mid Level.

    Conduct QA on all email and SMS campaigns and journeys in Iterable prior to launch to ensure every element is configured correctly and functions as intended.

    Verify campaign and journey names against Winona’s naming conventions (name, year, event, medium and audience).

    Review journey configuration, including start tiles, suppressions, scheduled send dates and times, tile logic and conditionals, entry limits, exit rules and journey event tracking.

    Confirm that monthly and recurring journeys are refreshed with updated start tiles prior to each send.

    Verify that campaign labels are applied correctly (audience, segments, category, goal and month/year).

    Confirm that the appropriate conversion events are assigned for each campaign type: prospect, customer upsell, Shop, community and live event campaigns.

    Review delivery settings, including quiet hours, send time optimization, frequency caps and performance alerts.

    Verify that link tracking is configured correctly, including Google Analytics, UTM parameters and custom link parameters.

    Review sender details: message type, from name, from email and reply-to address.

    Review email templates against Winona’s brand and design standards, including fonts, sizing, padding, CTA button styling, link formatting and footers.

    Test all links, CTA buttons and image links, and confirm that images include alt text.

    Proofread copy for accuracy, consistency and formatting.

    Send and review test proofs in light and dark mode on iOS and Android, across both Gmail and Apple Mail.

    Coordinate SMS test sends with the appropriate team members prior to testing.

    Conduct QA on email touchpoints that connect to Shopify, such as Shop campaigns and checkout-related flows, to ensure a seamless end-to-end experience.

    Follow and help maintain internal templating documentation, QA checklists and the HTML template library.

    Communicate issues, errors and inconsistencies to the lifecycle team clearly and promptly, and track them through resolution.

    Recommend improvements to QA processes and standards on an ongoing basis.

    At least 3 years of experience performing QA within an ESP like Iterable or similar platforms.

    Working knowledge of HTML and CSS for email.

    Exceptional attention to detail and consistent checklist execution.

    Understanding of how emails render across clients, devices and dark mode.

    Clear written communication for reporting issues.

    Proficiency with Handlebars or dynamic content personalization.

    Shopify experience, particularly with checkout and order flows.

    Experience with email testing tools such as Litmus or Email on Acid.

    Familiarity with Google Analytics and UTM tracking.

    Experience with ClickUp or similar project management tools.

    Knowledge of SMS best practices and compliance standards (CAN-SPAM, CASL).

    As a full-time independent contractor, you’ll enjoy:.

    Remote-first, work wherever you choose.

    Paid non-working holidays per country of residence.

    Pro-rated 13th-month bonus in select regions.

    Financial support for online courses.

    Fun and casual work environment.

    Employee engagement activities and virtual gatherings.

    It has been revealed that we are a diverse, global team! 🌍.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This is TVNewser’s basic cable network ranker and cable news report for the week of November 9, 2026.

    As expected, the three cable networks could not maintain their midterm election-week momentum, declining in total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo during primetime and total day.

    In a recent development, viewer interest remained high during the just-concluded week, driven by the breaking news of the FAA issuing a nationwide airplane groundstop on Friday, Nov. 13. Fox News was the most-watched network in total viewers on that day, while CNN finished on top in the prized demo.

    Interestingly, the FAA breaking news kept CNN in first place in the primetime demo for the second week in a row.

    According to Nielsen Big Data + Panel, for the week of Nov. 9, Fox News averaged 1.584 million total viewers and 109,000 A25-54 viewers during primetime. The network saw losses of 15% in total viewers and 33% in the demo compared with the prior week (the week beginning Nov. 2).

    During total day viewing, Fox News averaged 1.018 million total viewers and 93,000 A25-54 viewers. Based on the previous week’s average, the network was down by 9% in total viewers and 25% in the demo.

    Sources indicate that fox News remained second in total primetime viewership and slipped from third to fourth in demo viewership among all basic cable networks. During total day, it remained first in total viewers and was in third place in the total day demo.

    Industry observers note that MS NOW averaged 1.077 million total viewers and 109,000 viewers in the A25-54 demo for the week that just concluded. The network dropped by 30% in total viewers and 52% in the demo compared with its prior-week primetime average.

    In a recent development, during total day, MS NOW averaged 674,000 total viewers and 73,000 demo viewers. It was down 27% in total viewers and 42% in the demo compared with the network’s average the prior week.

    It has been revealed that among all basic cable networks, MS NOW continued to be in third in total primetime viewers and fell from fourth to ninth in the demo. It ranked third in total viewers and was sixth in the total day demo.

    According to recent reports, CNN averaged 802,000 total primetime viewers and 160,000 demo viewers. It saw declines of 40% in total viewers and 57% in the demo compared to the previous week.

    During total day, the network had 530,000 total viewers and 85,000 demo viewers. For CNN, total viewers were down 29%, and demo viewers were down 49% during this daypart.

    Among all cable networks, CNN remained in fourth place in total viewers and was the No. 3 network in the demo during primetime. It continued to be in fourth in total day among total viewers and was in the same position in the demo.

    Compared to their performance during the same period a year ago:.

    Industry observers note that fox News held 9 of the 15 spots among the week’s most-watched cable news shows, with The Five in first place with 2.562 million total viewers at 5 p.m. ET. MS NOW’s top show was the 9 p.m. ET Monday airing of The Rachel Maddow Show in fourth place with 1.904 million total viewers. MS NOW had a total of six programs in the top 15 for the just-concluded week.

    The 15 top spots in the Adults 25-54 demo were populated with shows from all three cable networks. CNN’s Anderson Cooper 360, airing weeknights at 8 p.m. ET, was in first place with 229,000 demo viewers. CNN had a total of five shows in the top 15. Fox News’ Jesse Watters Primetime, airing weeknights at 8 p.m. ET, finished second with 223,000 demo viewers. Fox News had seven shows on the chart. Finally, MS NOW’s The Rachel Maddow Show was the network’s top show, with 166,000 demo viewers, ranking 12th. MS NOW had four shows in the chart.

    Learn our default setups, decision log and the core and vendor systems around your product.

    Experience with self-managed or on-premises software where vendor visibility is limited.

    Nice to have: familiarity with process orchestration or Camunda's customer base.

    Storage Platform Engineer at Supabase

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Supabase runs millions of Postgres databases, and storage performance is now one of the biggest levers on how fast, reliable, and affordable they are.
    • As the senior engineer driving storage, you'll own this effort end to end: the architecture and build-vs-buy decisions, integration into our compute platform, and operating the system in production.
    • Recent findings suggest that your first goal is raw Postgres I/O performance at scale.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase runs millions of Postgres databases, and storage performance is now one of the biggest levers on how fast, reliable, and affordable they are. We're building a software-defined, NVMe-over-Fabrics storage platform underneath Supabase Postgres. Postgres stays unmodified, and the fresh layer delivers near-local-NVMe performance with the durability and flexibility of networked storage.

    As the senior engineer driving storage, you'll own this effort end to end: the architecture and build-vs-buy decisions, integration into our compute platform, and operating the system in production.

    Recent findings suggest that your first goal is raw Postgres I/O performance at scale. In the longer term, the layer you build will provide the block-level snapshots and copy-on-write clones behind database branching, fast restores, and instant resizes. Because it's software-defined, it will also travel with us as we expand beyond a single cloud provider into multi-cloud and colocated infrastructure.

    It has been revealed that this is a foundational, high-ownership role. You'll set the technical direction for storage at Supabase and help grow the team around it.

    Lead the architecture of Supabase's NVMe-oF storage platform, including evaluating and deciding between adopting existing software-defined storage and building on SPDK.

    Integrate networked block storage into our Kubernetes-based compute platform through CSI drivers and custom controllers, covering provisioning, attach/detach, resizing, and migration.

    Make Postgres fast on networked storage by profiling and tuning the full I/O path, from fsync, WAL, and checkpoints through the kernel block layer, NVMe/TCP, and the network.

    Design for durability and availability, including replication or erasure coding, failure domains, failover, and data-integrity verification.

    Build I/O isolation and QoS so that noisy neighbors can't degrade other tenants.

    Set performance and reliability SLOs, and build the benchmarking and observability to hold the system to them.

    Design the layer for block-level snapshots and copy-on-write clones, laying the groundwork for database branching.

    Keep the platform portable across AWS, other clouds, and bare-metal/colo.

    Write design docs, mentor engineers, and work closely with the Compute, Branching, Postgres, and Multicloud teams.

    Participate in on-call rotations, incident response, and post-incident reviews.

    Resolve escalated support challenges, while also identifying and resolving systemic issues across the platform.

    Have 7+ years of software engineering experience, including significant time building and operating storage systems in production.

    Have built or operated distributed or software-defined block storage (for example Ceph RBD, Lightbits, Simplyblock, Portworx, LINSTOR/DRBD, or an in-house system).

    Have hands-on experience with NVMe/TCP or NVMe-oF, including targets, initiators, multipath, and failover behavior.

    Have a deep understanding of Linux storage internals: the block layer, io_uring, page cache, O_DIRECT and fsync semantics, filesystems, and device-mapper.

    Write strong systems code in Go, plus C, C++, or Rust.

    Measure performance rigorously with fio, pgbench, eBPF, and perf, and can explain latency down to its individual components.

    Understand durability tradeoffs between replication, erasure coding, and consistency under failure.

    Have led technical direction on a complex system: design docs, tradeoffs, and bringing others along.

    Have experience with Kubernetes controllers and/or CSI drivers.

    Have been on call for large production systems.

    Communicate clearly in writing and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Experience implementing block-level snapshots, thin provisioning, or copy-on-write cloning.

    Postgres internals knowledge (WAL, buffer manager, checkpointer), or familiarity with OrioleDB.

    Experience with AWS networking and instance storage at scale (ENA, placement, bandwidth limits).

    Experience running storage on bare metal or in colo.

    Contributions to open source storage projects or the Linux kernel storage stack.

    Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Sources indicate that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Once a year, the entire tech giant gathers in a fresh city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Industry observers note that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • In a recent development, we’re looking for a Software Engineer, Postgres Tooling to join our CLI team and help build the open-source tools developers use to change their Postgres schemas safely.
    • Given two databases, or a database and a folder of SQL files describing the schema you want, pg-delta works out the differences and generates the migration to get from one to the other.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    In a recent development, we’re looking for a Software Engineer, Postgres Tooling to join our CLI team and help build the open-source tools developers use to change their Postgres schemas safely. You’ll join as a co-maintainer of pg-delta, our schema diff and migration engine, and grow into leading it.

    Given two databases, or a database and a folder of SQL files describing the schema you want, pg-delta works out the differences and generates the migration to get from one to the other. It powers supabase db diff, db pull, and declarative schemas, and it runs underneath Supabase’s platform, branching, and AI agent workflows. Every migration it generates is verified on a throwaway clone before it’s trusted, and it’s tested against 331 scenarios on PostgreSQL 14–18. We’re now working toward a stable, standalone 1.0 release for any Postgres developer, on Supabase or not.

    According to recent reports, this is a correctness-first role. The SQL this tool generates runs against production databases, so privilege safety and avoiding data loss are non-negotiable. It’s a great fit for someone who loves Postgres at the catalog level, enjoys compiler-style problems, and thrives in async, fast-paced environments.

    Co-maintain pg-delta: review and merge changes, including PRs written by AI agents, and grow into its lead maintainer.

    Own correctness: triage bug reports from GitHub and support, fix diff and dependency-ordering bugs, and extend test coverage across Postgres versions.

    Make sure generated migrations are privilege-safe and never silently lose data, by detecting destructive changes and rewriting them into safe equivalents where possible.

    Help take pg-delta to a stable 1.0: a public API with a semver contract, documentation, and broader coverage of Postgres extensions.

    Work with the open-source community: triage concerns, review outside contributions, and say no gracefully when a request doesn’t fit.

    Work with the teams across Supabase that build on pg-delta, so migrations are generated and run the same way everywhere.

    Write the design docs and technical strategy that set the tool’s direction, working async across teams.

    Sources indicate that share the CLI team’s on-call rotation. Weekdays are covered follow-the-sun, and because we ship packaged software that people can roll back, pages are rare.

    Have 8+ years of experience as a software engineer, including deep, hands-on work with PostgreSQL.

    Know Postgres internals at the catalog level: pg_catalog, pg_depend, object ownership, grants and default privileges, RLS policies, and extension membership.

    Understand DDL and migration semantics: which changes take locks, which can’t run inside a transaction, how dependencies determine ordering, and how to spot a destructive change.

    Treat a migration that silently loosens access as a top-severity bug.

    Write strong TypeScript, and design tests for correctness, such as differential, property-based, or corpus testing across multiple Postgres versions.

    Are comfortable with compiler-style problems: dependency graphs, topological ordering, cycle handling, and diffing.

    Can confidently review complex changes in an intricate codebase, including AI-generated PRs.

    Have owned software in production with users in the loop: staged rollouts, error monitoring, and triaging real bug reports.

    Have led a technical project across several teams, from an ambiguous start to production.

    Communicate clearly in writing and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Nice to have, roughly in order of how much they’d help:.

    Have built or maintained schema diff or migration tooling (such as migra, pg-schema-diff, Atlas, pgroll, sqitch, Prisma Migrate, or Flyway/Liquibase), or worked with pg_dump internals.

    Open-source maintainer experience: API contracts, semver, documentation, and community triage.

    Familiarity with Postgres extensions such as pg_cron, pgmq, pg_partman, vault, pg_net, pgvector, or PostGIS.

    Contributions to Postgres itself, or authorship of a Postgres extension.

    Experience with Supabase or another managed Postgres platform.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    #7923. Redesigned Microsoft Copilot Will Build Apps and Work on Its Own

    📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (759 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Redesigned Microsoft Copilot Will Build Apps and Work on Its Own

    📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Micorosft has announced that it's redesigning Copilot, the company's all-encompassing AI assistant, so users can hand off complex tasks, build tools by describing what they need, and assign work to an agent that keeps going after they log off.
    • It has been revealed that the newly introduced Copilot experience has three main parts: Home, Code, and Autopilot.
    • Home puts Chat and Copilot Cowork together.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Micorosft has announced that it's redesigning Copilot, the company's all-encompassing AI assistant, so users can hand off complex tasks, build tools by describing what they need, and assign work to an agent that keeps going after they log off.

    It has been revealed that the newly introduced Copilot experience has three main parts: Home, Code, and Autopilot. It also brings Word, Excel, and PowerPoint into the Copilot app. For users, the pitch is simple: Start a task in one place and stay there as it grows from a quick question into a document, an app, or a longer-running project. Most of the new capabilities are still rolling out or in preview.

    Home puts Chat and Copilot Cowork together. Chat remains the place for quick answers, research, and drafts. Cowork handles work a user wants to delegate, such as preparing a briefing or pulling together a response to a request for proposals. Microsoft noted Copilot eventually will route requests to Chat, Cowork, or Code on its own.

    In a recent development, office in Copilot will allow customers to create a Word document, Excel workbook, or PowerPoint deck without leaving that experience. The files remain editable in the regular Office apps, and colleagues can work on them at the same time. Someone building a presentation, for example, could draw on a workbook, draft the slides, and keep refining both files from within Copilot.

    Sources indicate that code is aimed at people who need a tool but might never open a development environment. A user can describe a tracker, dashboard, app, or workflow in plain language and have Copilot build it. Microsoft calls these "small, purpose-built solutions." The feature uses the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot and runs in a sandboxed environment. A separate Copilot Managed Runtime, now in preview, lets organizations host and share the resulting apps within Microsoft 365.

    Then there is Autopilot, previously known as Scout. It is designed for work that does not end with a single response: following a discussion, checking in with stakeholders, or keeping a project moving over several days. "Give it a name, a role, and a goal," Microsoft said. Autopilot runs in the cloud and has its own identity, memory, and workspace in the customer's tenant. Microsoft said its actions are subject to permissions, auditing, and organizational controls.

    Those longer-running tasks also change how customers pay for Copilot. In a separate pricing post, Microsoft said everyday work in Chat and Microsoft 365 apps will remain covered by a per-user subscription. Cowork, Code, and Autopilot will be billed separately through usage-based Copilot Credits. A Copilot user subscription will still be needed to access those features.

    Sources indicate that for enterprise customers, the features that charge by usage will stay off until an admin sets up a spending policy in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Microsoft said there will be no charges before then. Admins can set budgets for the whole organization or for specific groups, limit how much individual owners can spend, and get alerts when costs approach a set amount. Reports will show who is using the features and which tasks are driving costs.

    Microsoft is bringing Code and Copilot Managed Runtime under those cost controls alongside Cowork. Copilot Studio agents are expected to follow in October. Before turning the features on for more employees, IT departments will need to decide who can use them, how much they can spend and which tasks are worth the extra cost.

    Home and Code will begin rolling out through Microsoft's Frontier early access program in the coming weeks. Code's Frontier rollout starts at the end of September, when Autopilot also expands to private preview.

    For more information, visit the Microsoft site.

    Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

    AI Leaders Warn of Risks at United Nations Security Council Briefing

    📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face recently joined AI researcher Yoshua Bengio at the United Nations headquarters in Newly introduced York on September 23 to warn the UN Security Council about the security risks of increasingly capable AI.
    • They did not offer a single initiative for managing those risks.
    • France, which held the Security Council's rotating presidency, convened the meeting on AI and international security.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face recently joined AI researcher Yoshua Bengio at the United Nations headquarters in Newly introduced York on September 23 to warn the UN Security Council about the security risks of increasingly capable AI.

    They did not offer a single initiative for managing those risks. Bengio called for licensing and independent safety reviews. OpenAI's Sam Altman proposed common standards that countries could adopt through their own laws. Anthropic's Dario Amodei urged AI developers to slow down when safety work cannot keep pace. Hugging Face's Clément Delangue warned that limiting access to capable systems could leave defenders at a disadvantage.

    France, which held the Security Council's rotating presidency, convened the meeting on AI and international security. The discussion exposed a difficult question for governments: how to oversee technology that crosses borders when countries disagree about who should set the rules.

    According to recent reports, bengio, co-chair of the UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, challenged the idea that competition forces companies to keep building more powerful systems. "The race is not a law of nature: it is the product of choices," he said in his published remarks. "They've told us they would slow down if they could. They can.".

    According to recent reports, he called on developers to show independent experts that frontier systems are safe to train and deploy. He also proposed incident reporting, licensing, and liability insurance. Bengio identified catastrophic misuse, concentrated power, and the loss of human control as risks that require international cooperation.

    In a recent development, altman acknowledged the danger of moving too rapidly. "We have unilaterally slowed down in the past. We will do so in the future," he said, according to remarks published by OpenAI. Decisions about AI's direction "cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," he added.

    Sources indicate that altman proposed complementary national and international standards to measure frontier AI capabilities, assess risks, and test safeguards. He said countries should be able to compare evidence and verify commitments. He also called for faster reporting of serious incidents and secure channels for sharing emerging threats. Such standards should accommodate both open and closed models without favoring established companies, he said.

    Industry observers note that amodei made a more direct commitment about the pace of Anthropic's releases: "We will slow down as much as necessary," he told the council. He identified two principal concerns: the misuse of AI to develop biological weapons and the possibility that advanced systems could outstrip developers' ability to control them.

    The Anthropic chief proposed placing outside evaluators inside AI companies with access comparable to employees. He suggested that governments begin with a narrow agreement against using AI to make biological weapons, then develop ways to evaluate models and verify commitments across borders. He also called for common testing standards and a system for notifying other countries of significant AI incidents.

    Recent findings suggest that delangue drew on a July incident in which Hugging Face disclosed an AI agent cyberattack. He called for stronger monitoring and disclosure, but argued that safety also depends on giving defenders access to capable tools. The central danger, he mentioned, was "asymmetry of powerful AI" between attackers and defenders, large companies and everyone else, and wealthy countries and the rest of the world. His team used an open-source model while responding to the attack, he said.

    Industry observers note that the U.S. government opposed a broader international regulatory role. White House science adviser Michael Kratsios told the council that countries should develop their own ability to use and govern the technology. In the U.S. statement, he rejected new global governance structures and used the phrase "superintelligence, formerly known as AI," adopting President Donald Trump's terminology from his General Assembly speech the previous day.

    The four AI briefers differed on how far oversight should go and how widely capable systems should be available. They agreed on a narrower point: Governments need better ways to understand what advanced AI systems can do and to detect when safeguards fail.

He also co-scripted the documentary film Silicon Valley: A 100 Year Renaissance, which aired on PBS. He can be reached at [email protected].

    Cybercriminals are moving away from mass phishing scams and focusing on more targeted attacks, often using trusted websites and services to trick victims, according to a newly introduced report from KnowBe4.

    Industry observers note that AI is moving beyond assisting cybercriminals and beginning to operate within live attacks, according to a recent report from Check Point Research. The technology is making sophisticated capabilities faster and more accessible while creating newly introduced security risks for businesses deploying their own AI systems.

    Class CrunchLabs, the suite of free curriculum resources from NASA engineer turned YouTube science communicator Mark Rober, has released its first two courses on YouTube.

    Designed in partnership with the National Science Teaching Association, the standards-aligned "Carnival of Collisions: Contact Forces" and "Mission MagLev: Electric & Magentic Forces" courses offer free video lessons, guided activities, and supplemental teaching resources for grades 6-8.

    It has been revealed that class CrunchLabs was released last year to offer free hands-on science curriculum resources including teaching guides, classroom slides, student readings and handouts, assessments, and instructional videos featuring Rober alongside "Science Bob" Pflugfelder, celebrity guests, and student co-hosts. The initiative was backed by a $7.2 million grant to create the CrunchLabs.org Foundation, a nonprofit "dedicated to revolutionizing science education in a way that promotes critical thinking and inspires lasting curiosity and confidence in STEM," according to a news announcement at the time.

    The organization aims to roll out additional courses on YouTube over time, with the ultimate goal of posting more than 1,000 science videos in 34 languages.

    #7904. OpenAI Getting Rid of Custom GPTs and Moving to Plugin Architecture

    📅 05 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (635 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    OpenAI Getting Rid of Custom GPTs and Moving to Plugin Architecture

    📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (635 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OpenAI has confirmed it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a upcoming plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.
    • Custom GPT retirement is currently scheduled for Dec.
    • In a recent development, for affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OpenAI has confirmed it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a upcoming plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.

    Custom GPT retirement is currently scheduled for Dec. 11, 2026, although the organization claims timing and migration availability can vary by account and workspace.

    In a recent development, for affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct. 26 for ending creation of new Custom GPTs. Qualifying Enterprise customers with approved deferrals can continue using them until Feb. 11, 2027.

    OpenAI has changed its UI to make GPTs less prominent, and when customers choose to try creating a latest Custom GPT, they are now prompted with an option to create a plugin instead.

    Rather than maintaining separate customized versions of ChatGPT, OpenAI is shifting customization toward plugins that can package reusable instructions, reference material, and connections to outside services.

    Sources indicate that under OpenAI's plugin architecture, a plugin can include one or more skills containing instructions and resources for repeatable workflows, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing tools and external systems, or both. ChatGPT and Codex share a universal plugin directory, although some capabilities can remain specific to a particular environment.

    For organizations, that makes the change more than a simple renaming exercise. A firm could package recurring workflows into skills while using MCP servers or connected apps to give those workflows access to enterprise systems and data.

    In a recent development, openAI claims creators will be able to migrate an existing GPT through the My GPTs interface. The GPT's instructions become a skill in the replacement plugin, while knowledge files are copied into plugin reference files and connected apps can be carried over.

    Industry observers note that not everything transfers automatically. Existing GPT conversations do not migrate, the selected model does not carry over, and Custom Actions may have to be rebuilt using an available app or a custom MCP server.

    Sources indicate that sharing also changes. Migrated plugins start private, existing GPT owners do not automatically receive access to the replacement, and prior sharing settings do not carry over.

    OpenAI is also cautioning organizations against assuming that migration will preserve behavior exactly. "A migrated plugin may respond differently," the company notes, recommending that owners retest familiar prompts, reference-material use, required output formats, and integrations before relying on the replacement.

    In a recent development, that warning has contributed to pushback from some GPT builders, who argue that plugins do not fully reproduce the dedicated and predictable environment of a Custom GPT. Other complaints have focused on sharing, migration complexity, and differences in how migrated workflows use instructions and reference material.

    Industry observers note that despite those concerns, OpenAI is clearly consolidating around plugins as its common mechanism for extending its AI products. Its developer documentation now describes plugins as packages people can "discover, install, share, and publish" across ChatGPT and Codex, replacing the separate-custom-assistant model with reusable AI capabilities that can be combined with enterprise tools and services.

    For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

    David Ramel is an editor and writer at Converge 360.

    #7901. AI Ambitions Are Running Into a Network Infrastructure Trust Problem

    📅 05 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (812 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    AI Ambitions Are Running Into a Network Infrastructure Trust Problem

    📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.
    • Sources indicate that the research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years.
    • The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.

    Sources indicate that the research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years. Among respondents whose initiatives were affected, AI and data-driven projects were the most cited, at 49%. That put AI ahead of security and compliance programs at 44%, digital transformation at 42%, and cloud migration at 38%.

    The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.

    According to recent reports, all respondents worked for organizations with more than 2,000 employees and influenced network strategy across data centers, cloud, and connectivity. Of those surveyed, 66% had final sign-off responsibility. The results suggest that as organizations pursue increasingly data-intensive AI projects, confidence in the network infrastructure supporting them could become another deployment obstacle.

    Sources indicate that on the surface, Arelion found little evidence of a trust crisis. A total of 93% of respondents said they largely or completely trust their current network provider, while 83% said that trust has strengthened over time.

    In a recent development, the picture changes when respondents are asked about a serious network incident. Only 15% mentioned they have complete confidence in their provider's ability to swiftly detect and address such a problem. Another 42% said their provider seriously lets them down anywhere from a few times a year to monthly or more frequently.

    Recent findings suggest that those concerns have consequences beyond the network itself. Responding organizations have delayed, scaled back, or stopped strategic initiatives because of provider trust concerns, while others have added resiliency or risk-mitigation measures.

    AI and data projects were the most affected among respondents reporting an impact, as organizations try to move AI from experimentation into larger production deployments.

    It has been revealed that A serious provider failure could also have substantial consequences. Forty percent of respondents stated such an event would cause major operational disruption, while 18% anticipated significant financial loss or severe financial or reputational damage.

    In a recent development, another tension runs through Arelion's findings. Enterprises need networks they can trust to support AI projects, but many of the same decision-makers are concerned about AI's growing role inside those networks. A total of 54% of respondents identified AI and automation in network management and security as the factors most likely to negatively affect network trust over the next three years. That ranked ahead of data sovereignty expectations and geopolitical instability, both at 39%, and regulatory requirements and quantum computing threats to current encryption standards, both at 38%.

    At the same time, respondents aren't rejecting AI as a network technology. Proactive AI-driven fault prediction was among the capabilities they noted would matter most to future trust, alongside stronger built-in security, greater accountability, and responsive support. That leaves enterprises in an unusual position: AI is increasing their dependence on digital infrastructure while also raising questions about how that infrastructure itself is managed.

    Arelion has an interest in emphasizing the importance of network-provider trust, and the survey reflects the views specifically of network decision-makers at large enterprises. Still, the findings point to an infrastructure consideration that can get lost amid the rush to adopt newly introduced AI models and agents. AI projects ultimately depend on the networks, cloud environments, data centers, and connectivity beneath them. If organizations lack confidence in that foundation, access to better AI models alone won't remove the obstacle.

    "Trust is influencing which strategic initiatives move forward, how organizations manage risk, and which providers they choose to work with," noted Mattias Fridström, Vice President at Arelion. "As businesses become increasingly reliant on digital infrastructure, enterprises are looking for network providers that can demonstrate transparency, accountability, and operational excellence, not just availability.".

    The full report is available for download here at the Arelion site (registration required).

    📅 07 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (505 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Research: Lack of Specialized Infrastructure Is a Top AI Adoption Challenge

    📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research Digital Realty.
    • The Global Data Insights Survey 2026 points to a widening mix of infrastructure models behind enterprise AI.
    • The research is based on an online survey of 2,131 IT decision-makers across 19 countries, and 11 industries, conducted from Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research Digital Realty. Forty percent of survey respondents cited a lack of specialized infrastructure required by AI as a main challenge to adopting a formal AI strategy, up from 9% in the tech giant's 2024 research.

    The Global Data Insights Survey 2026 points to a widening mix of infrastructure models behind enterprise AI. Half of respondents host AI models in private clouds, 86% are pursuing or exploring sovereign AI, 92% tie data-location strategy to their AI prepares, and 88% follow a distributed-data approach.

    The research is based on an online survey of 2,131 IT decision-makers across 19 countries, and 11 industries, conducted from Nov. 23, 2025, through Feb. 4, 2026.

    It has been revealed that organizations also appear to be shifting from AI planning toward execution. The share actively executing AI to achieve operational efficiency or reduce costs rose from 27% in 2024 to 37% this year. Only 3% reported no measurable ROI to date, while 63% expect returns within the next six months to two years.

    Specialized infrastructure led the survey's list of AI adoption challenges at 40%, followed by regulatory and personal-data concerns at 35%. Data availability and quality, storage capacity, interconnection, compute resources, and staffing also ranked as significant constraints.

    Those requirements are also shaping workload placement. Integration with existing IT or data infrastructure ranked first at 43%, while regulatory compliance and performance were each cited by 37%. Data proximity, sovereignty, sustainability, cost, and intellectual property protection also factored into hosting decisions.

    Private cloud features prominently across the report's AI hosting categories, but enterprises are clearly using a mix of private cloud, public cloud, on-premises infrastructure, and colocation. Private cloud accounted for 50% of custom-built AI model hosting and 47% for open source or fine-tuned large language models (LLMs).

    Recent findings suggest that sovereignty is another part of that placement decision. Thirty-two percent consider sovereign AI — in which data and AI models remain within a single national or regulatory jurisdiction — a requirement, while another 54% are exploring it. The findings point toward hybrid environments in which infrastructure location, governance and data control increasingly overlap.

    #7893. OpenAI Intros Dots, AI Agents that Continue Working Between User Conversations

    📅 07 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (705 w)

    OpenAI Intros Dots, AI Agents that Continue Working Between User Conversations

    📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OpenAI has introduced Dots, GPT-6 Astra-powered agents that run on their own cloud computers, using connected applications to carry on with assignments between conversations and incorporating owners' feedback as they go.
    • According to recent reports, openAI is also previewing specialist Dots for organizations, with separate identities and credentials for defined responsibilities.
    • The broader ambition seems to be to make delegation last beyond a chat session.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OpenAI has introduced Dots, GPT-6 Astra-powered agents that run on their own cloud computers, using connected applications to carry on with assignments between conversations and incorporating owners' feedback as they go.

    According to recent reports, openAI is also previewing specialist Dots for organizations, with separate identities and credentials for defined responsibilities. Those enterprise deployments are beginning with focused pilots. The manufacturer is working with Microsoft on integration with Agent 365's governance and security controls.

    The broader ambition seems to be to make delegation last beyond a chat session. That change could reduce the need to repeatedly explain a project. It also makes supervision a continuing obligation: An instruction that was appropriate yesterday may no longer fit today's circumstances.

    One important distinction appears in OpenAI's privacy and safety FAQ. Disconnecting an application stops new access through that connection, but does not delete information already incorporated into a Dot's context.

    Sources indicate that owners currently cannot inspect or directly edit individual Dot memories. Deleting a Dot deletes its own context, while files and conversations it created remain separately stored. Plugin permissions are shared across Dots, ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex.

    For an organization, that creates two related governance questions: what an agent can retrieve now, and what it already knows. Revoking a connection addresses the first without necessarily resolving the second.

    Sources indicate that openAI's safety account distinguishes authorized tasks that continue in the background from unsolicited "proactive research." The latter uses tools restricted to reading permitted sources. Those research tasks cannot directly send messages, change connected application content, or control a browser or desktop. Any subsequent action must pass the usual rules and checks.

    A separate system, Auto-review, checks certain planned actions against instructions and safety requirements. OpenAI indicates the agent cannot modify the controls enforcing those checks.

    "Dots can still make mistakes," the company cautions.

    Sources indicate that openAI's Dots system-card appendix acknowledges that persistence and multi-agent systems are not new. Its evaluations examine how continuing work affects authorization boundaries.

    Industry observers note that in one test involving successive related tasks, moderate scope violations increased from 8.6% to 19.7% when the number of intervening tasks doubled from five to 10. Examples included carrying information between unrelated tasks or editing a shared document beyond the intended scope. The company reported no severe breaches or exfiltration in that evaluation.

    Sources indicate that these are controlled test results, not measured failure rates in customer deployments. They nevertheless identify a problem that a successful demonstration cannot settle: whether an agent keeps the right boundaries as its workload accumulates.

    It has been revealed that according to OpenAI's DevDay recap, Dots are available to Pro and Business Premium customers in eligible markets. Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare access is an administrator-enabled beta, off by default.

    Recent findings suggest that the operational question is how organizations will keep delegated authority current. A continuing assignment needs a human owner who can revise its scope and decide when to stop it. Otherwise, the convenience of leaving work with an agent can outlast the reason it was authorized.

    For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

    #7889. Survey Identifies Data Governance Enforcement Gap for Agentic AI Tools

    📅 07 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (810 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Survey Identifies Data Governance Enforcement Gap for Agentic AI Tools

    📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to a new survey from identity security organization Delinea, 99.7% of IT and security leaders remarked their organization has a formal policy governing what data AI tools and agents are permitted to access.
    • That disconnect is at the center of Delinea's fall 2026 Identity Security Report, "The AI Enforcement Gap," which suggests companies have made quick progress establishing AI governance but have not necessarily built the technical controls needed to enforce it.
    • The findings come from a pair of surveys covering 2,254 IT and security leaders and 2,250 non-IT employees at organizations with at least 500 employees across the U.S, U.K, Germany, Australia, Singapore, UAE, France, and India.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to a new survey from identity security organization Delinea, 99.7% of IT and security leaders remarked their organization has a formal policy governing what data AI tools and agents are permitted to access. Yet only about 51% said AI access is checked against those policies in real time. Perhaps more worrying is that only 19% said their organization could detect in real time when an agent last accessed data outside its intended scope.

    That disconnect is at the center of Delinea's fall 2026 Identity Security Report, "The AI Enforcement Gap," which suggests companies have made quick progress establishing AI governance but have not necessarily built the technical controls needed to enforce it.

    The findings come from a pair of surveys covering 2,254 IT and security leaders and 2,250 non-IT employees at organizations with at least 500 employees across the U.S, U.K, Germany, Australia, Singapore, UAE, France, and India.

    All the organizations were using or piloting AI, while the employees surveyed used at least one AI tool for work.

    The problem becomes more consequential as companies move from AI tools that primarily respond to consumers toward agents capable of taking actions on their behalf.

    Eighty-seven percent of IT and security respondents remarked their organization had experienced or suspected of an incident during the past year in which an AI tool or agent accessed sensitive information beyond what was required for its task.

    Delinea's research also suggests companies are giving agents access that can persist longer than necessary. Only 58% of IT and security leaders noted they have mechanisms that automatically revoke or expire AI access when a session ends, and those controls do not necessarily cover every agent or tool. Forty-two percent said many agent credentials remain active until an audit.

    Industry observers note that agents also are not always receiving their own narrowly defined permissions. Half of IT leaders said their organizations use the employee's existing permissions as a boundary for what an agent can access. That can effectively hand an agent years of accumulated access belonging to the person who launched it.

    According to recent reports, that is particularly significant because an AI agent does not necessarily behave like a traditional service account. A service account typically performs a predefined process, while an agent can choose different tools, actions and sequences at runtime depending on the situation.

    In a recent development, "Service accounts run fixed scripts," remarked Mike Albrecht, associate director in the Risk Advisory Practice at Cross Country Consulting. "An AI agent decides what actions it's going to take at runtime.".

    The enforcement problem is not limited to autonomous agents.

    Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that 76% of employees surveyed had bypassed formal approval at some point to use AI tools with company data, applications or systems. And 48% said they always or extensively use AI tools without going through formal approval.

    Meanwhile, 60% stated they had felt pressure to use AI with sensitive or confidential information even when they were not sure doing so was permitted.

    According to recent reports, executives were particularly likely to circumvent the process. Eighty-one percent of C-level respondents stated they always or regularly bypass AI access approval, compared with 33% of intermediate-level employees.

    The result is a widening gap between written AI governance and what companies can see and control. Delinea found that only 41% of IT leaders said all AI tools and agents accessing firm data are actively monitored. When an AI tool or agent went outside its intended scope, 55% said it took at least a day to detect the incident, while 30% said detection took four days or longer.

    That suggests the next phase of enterprise AI governance may depend less on writing additional rules and more on whether organizations can enforce existing ones while an agent is working.

    Sources indicate that "Most organizations cannot confidently answer three questions: What agents are running in our environment? What can they access? What have they actually done?" remarked Delinea CEO Art Gilliland. "An agent can begin a session with legitimate access and drift into something it was never meant to do.".

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that we love fisherman sweaters for the same reason we love a great martini: They’re classic, and they’re comforting.
    • Now, it’s crucial to remember that when it comes to the backstory of most garments, there tends to be a lot of lore mixed in with the genuine history.
    • In 2026, you probably don’t need a fisherman sweater to keep you warm while you’re on the water off Ireland’s west coast.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that we love fisherman sweaters for the same reason we love a great martini: They’re classic, and they’re comforting. A proper fisherman knit brings the whole winter wardrobe into alignment. The chunky texture instantly upgrades jeans and boots, warmth doesn’t sacrifice style, and that easy, rugged-prep vibe that works at the office as well as it does on the couch. In other words, it’s the rare cold-weather staple that’s as practical as it is handsome.

    Now, it’s crucial to remember that when it comes to the backstory of most garments, there tends to be a lot of lore mixed in with the genuine history. That noted, here’s how the story generally goes. Traditional fisherman sweaters hail from Ireland, where in the late 1800s to the mid-1900s, they were popular for men who had to work long hours on fishing boats. Usually, fisherman sweaters were hand-knit by their wives or by local artisans, and they were always designed to be sturdy and warm, keeping the wind and chill out. Cable-knit patterns became popular for fisherman sweaters. You might know these sweaters as Aran sweaters, referencing the Aran Islands, where the textured design has become a specialty.

    In 2026, you probably don’t need a fisherman sweater to keep you warm while you’re on the water off Ireland’s west coast. (Or maybe you do! We don’t know your story.) However, you do need a fisherman sweater for the sheer coziness and looks they provide, though. Our favorite options of all time are below, tested and reviewed by Esquire editors (with some photographed on Esquire’s editor in chief, Michael Sebastian). Anyway, these fisherman sweaters are seriously making us want to take some fishing lessons. Anyone know where we can do that?

    In a recent development, you don’t need to break the bank for a high-quality fisherman sweater that’ll last you years to come. Quince is proof. Crafted from organic cotton, this thick, warm sweater is a perfect layering piece for winter—put a tee or a button-down underneath, a topcoat or a puffer on top, and you’re golden. The rib detailing offers some extra texture and style, and relaxed raglan sleeves offer more freedom of movement.

    It has been revealed that ok, so the pictured sweater is no longer in stock. The cable knit rollneck was seasonal, but there is always a fisherman-y option in the collection. Honestly, whichever J. Crew rollneck hits this bar at any point in time, that’s likely my favorite fisherman sweater of the moment.

    According to recent reports, L.L. Bean crafts a classic fisherman sweater to a tee. It has everything you’d want in the style: a thick, heavyweight fabric that carries some structure with it; a cable-knit design; and thick cotton yarn that keeps the chill out and the warmth in. This style is a go-to for something timeless without too much fuss or frill. It has a slim fit, so if you want something baggier, more classically cut, make sure to size up.

    It has been revealed that okay, hear me out—this isn’t your traditional fisherman sweater, but you can make a damn good excuse for Polo Ralph Lauren’s ultra-soft, ultra-luxe cable-knit sweater when you feel how unbelievably plush this is. This is the fisherman sweater you go to when you want something distinctly elevated and chic but you still want to have a cable-knit design and a fit you can dress down with joggers and slides.

    In a recent development, you may already know that we at Esquire have an affinity for shawl collar cardigans. With their laid-back Western vibes and classic Americana silhouette, shawl collar cardigans look handsome on just about any guy. One of our favorites is this fisherman style from Filson. It’s made from thick, warm cotton and features a classic button front and ribbing on the hem and cuffs.

    According to recent reports, if you, like commerce editor Luke Guillory, aren’t into the super chunky fisherman sweaters and are looking for something a little more lightweight that you can easily layer, this Buck Mason pick should be right up your alley. Luke has even endorsed the style, lauding the sweater for its warm yet lightweight feel, perfect not-too-boxy but not-too-slim cut, and durable cotton that can be machine washed and still not miss a beat.

    This gorgeous wool fisherman sweater is from Finisterre, a surf clothing brand from Cornwall, England, so it’s specifically made for cold, windy days on the water. It’s made from 100 percent heavyweight, pure latest wool with a natural crimp, which means it creates natural pockets of air to help insulate you (even if you’re not on the water). One writer states it’s one of his go-to winter sweaters.

    Brooks Brothers’ woolly sweater is so damn good I might just have to take up the art of fishing to pay proper tribute to it. With a soft and cozy yet breathable wool fabric and cable-knit pattern, this relaxed style puts a contemporary spin on the traditional fisherman sweater. It’s warm, soft, and stylish, and it looks just as good with dress pants and loafers as it does with jeans and sneakers.

    In a recent development, begg x Co’s Isla cashmere sweater is another fantastic, high-quality cashmere option. It’s just oppressively beautiful. Begg x Co operates its own mills in Scotland, which shows up in the world-class materials and construction, but the vibe isn’t overly capital-F-Fashion the way some French or Italian luxury brands can feel. It’s timeless, understated luxury. Made from 8‑ply cashmere, it lands in a perfect mid-weight sweet spot for fall and winter: substantial and warm without being bulky. It’s definitely quite pricey, but you’re paying for the highest level of quality and finish.

    According to recent reports, this sweater from Ghiaia Cashmere is divine, surprising considering the brand is based out of southern California. The mock neck is the star here—cozy without the bulk of a turtleneck—and the rich brown color is lovely (though it also comes in a clean cream if you want something lighter). A chest pocket adds a surprisingly practical touch, making it feel more functional than you’d ever expect a sweater to be.

    #7884. Industry News: Claude Intros Sonnet 5.5 with Model-Switching Cybersecurity Safeguards

    📅 08 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (541 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Claude Intros Sonnet 5.5 with Model-Switching Cybersecurity Safeguards

    📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthropic's new Claude release, Sonnet 5.5, brings cybersecurity safeguards that can change which model handles a request during a Claude conversation.
    • Sources indicate that according to Anthropic's explanation of model switching, automatic fallback is enabled by default in Claude.
    • The company identifies penetration testing and exploit generation among activities that may trigger cybersecurity fallbacks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Anthropic's new Claude release, Sonnet 5.5, brings cybersecurity safeguards that can change which model handles a request during a Claude conversation. Higher-risk tasks can fall back to Sonnet 5.

    Sources indicate that according to Anthropic's explanation of model switching, automatic fallback is enabled by default in Claude. Users receive a notice, and the answer is labeled with the model that provided it. The chat then stays on Sonnet 5 unless the user changes the selection.

    The company identifies penetration testing and exploit generation among activities that may trigger cybersecurity fallbacks. Source-code vulnerability scanning remains supported. Biology and reasoning-extraction safeguards can block requests outright, rather than route them elsewhere.

    The distinction matters operationally. A block stops the request; a fallback allows an attempt to continue with a different model. Neither outcome should be treated as interchangeable with completion by the model the user originally chose.

    Anthropic indicates Sonnet 5.5 generates output more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and can reduce cost per task by up to 30%, based on its testing. Token prices remain unchanged.

    Industry observers note that those claims describe performance under the organization's test conditions. An organization evaluating the service also needs to examine what happens when its own assignments encounter safeguards.

    Industry observers note that an internal pilot could record how often work is interrupted, whether fallback answers are usable, and when owners need help. Such measurements would give buyers a more relevant basis for deployment than assuming every task receives the advertised model's capabilities.

    Anthropic has declared intends to expand its Cyber Verification Program with tiered access for Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Mythos models. Its current program guidance explicitly excludes the two latest 5.5 models and indicates the expansion is forthcoming.

    Organizations should distinguish those planned arrangements from access available today.

    Sources indicate that the broader enterprise glitch is accountability. When an AI service changes models during an assignment, someone still needs to determine whether the resulting work is suitable. A visible handoff helps, but organizations must decide how employees should respond to it.

    For more information on Sonnet 5.5, go to the Anthropic site.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures.
    • According to recent reports, the research, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global, examines both the risks and potential benefits of the technologies.
    • Cloud-based storage, cloud-delivered applications, and cloud management infrastructure were the three most frequently cited asset types targeted by attackers, at 35%, 34%, and 32%, respectively.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures. The 2026 Thales Data Threat Report: Quantum & AI Trends, based on responses from 3,120 security and IT management professionals across 20 countries, found that 98% are considering how the two technologies affect each other. Thirty percent reported a significant increase in security budgets specifically for AI.

    According to recent reports, the research, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global, examines both the risks and potential benefits of the technologies. Fifty-seven percent believe quantum computing will enhance machine learning, while 54% expect it to enable advanced simulations of complex systems. The security findings span data governance, cloud infrastructure, and preparations for quantum-resistant encryption.

    Cloud-based storage, cloud-delivered applications, and cloud management infrastructure were the three most frequently cited asset types targeted by attackers, at 35%, 34%, and 32%, respectively. The report connects that exposure to the large datasets required for AI training and the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

    It has been revealed that organizations are also looking to cloud providers for protection: 67% reported investing in their cloud provider's AI-specific security tools, compared with 63% using an established security provider. Respondents could identify multiple sources of protection, including startups, large language model providers, and internally developed controls.

    It has been revealed that encryption coverage remains incomplete. Only 7% of organizations reported encrypting more than 80% of their sensitive cloud data, while 29% reported encrypting more than 60%. The report's chart puts the average share encrypted at 47% in 2026, down from 51% in 2025.

    The findings extend concerns raised in coverage of Thales' 2025 cloud security research, when AI security already ranked second to cloud security in spending priorities and 52% of respondents reported that AI security spending was displacing existing security budgets. The latest report again places AI security second, while its historical comparison indicates average sensitive cloud data encryption coverage falling from 51% in 2025 to 47% in 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that AI security was the second-highest prioritized security spending category overall, behind cloud security. But protecting data ranked much lower among the measures organizations use to judge AI projects: Reducing or managing risks of data loss or noncompliance placed sixth among seven success criteria, at 35%.

    In a recent development, improving customer experience led those measures at 68%, followed by reducing employee toil through greater task automation at 63%. Meanwhile, poor data quality or initial data governance was the leading inhibitor to AI adoption, cited by 65%; security risks from exposed data followed at 61%. Another 51% cited AI initiatives moving too swiftly to be properly secured.

    In an active social engineering campaign, cyber attackers are impersonating IT help desks and using fake passkey setup requests to compromise employee identities and gain access to enterprise cloud data.

    A newly introduced study from consulting firm KPMG found that while AI investment continues to grow, relatively few organizations consistently measure whether the technology's benefits justify its costs.

    Cybercriminals are moving away from mass phishing scams and focusing on more targeted attacks, often using trusted websites and services to trick victims, according to a latest report from KnowBe4.

    According to recent reports, AI is moving beyond assisting cybercriminals and beginning to operate within live attacks, according to a recent report from Check Point Research. The technology is making sophisticated capabilities faster and more accessible while creating fresh security risks for businesses deploying their own AI systems.

    #7874. Breaking: Flashpoint Receives Patent for Ransomware Risk Model, Tying Vulnerabilites to Likelihood of Attack

    📅 09 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (802 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Flashpoint Receives Patent for Ransomware Risk Model, Tying Vulnerabilites to Likelihood of Attack

    📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, cybersecurity company Flashpoint announced it has received U.S.
    • The patent comes at a time when security teams are confronting a growing vulnerability problem: Flashpoint's Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition tracked 21,667 vulnerability disclosures during the first half of 2026, an 8% increase.
    • Of those, 4,015, or around 19 percent, already had public or functional exploit code.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, cybersecurity company Flashpoint announced it has received U.S. Patent No. 12,705,360 for its Ransomware Risk model, a methodology designed to help security teams determine which newly disclosed vulnerabilities more closely resemble those historically used in ransomware attacks.

    The patent comes at a time when security teams are confronting a growing vulnerability problem: Flashpoint's Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition tracked 21,667 vulnerability disclosures during the first half of 2026, an 8% increase.

    Of those, 4,015, or around 19 percent, already had public or functional exploit code. Flashpoint also reported a 45 percent increase in Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) attacks during the period.

    It has been revealed that the patent was granted August 11 2026, although the underlying Ransomware Risk model isn't fresh. It has been available through Flashpoint Vulnerability Intelligence since 2022.

    The model addresses a basic vulnerability-management problem: severity and real-world ransomware risk aren't necessarily the same thing, because severity scores do not necessarily indicate which flaws attackers are most likely to target.

    It has been revealed that the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, or CVSS, measures how severe a vulnerability could be. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System, or EPSS, estimates the probability of exploitation more broadly.

    Flashpoint's Ransomware Risk model adds another dimension by comparing newly disclosed vulnerabilities with the characteristics of flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks.

    That could change where a vulnerability lands in an organization's patching queue. A lower-severity flaw might normally sit behind numerous critical vulnerabilities. But if its characteristics closely resemble vulnerabilities repeatedly targeted by ransomware operators, security teams may have reason to move it higher.

    "A severity score alone can't tell you which vulnerabilities pose the greatest real-world risk of exploitation by ransomware actors," Flashpoint CEO Josh Lefkowitz remarked. "Our patented Ransomware Risk model applies years of threat intelligence to that problem, giving customers an earlier signal and helping them prioritize based on how attackers actually operate.".

    The firm's midyear research also illustrates the scale of the prioritization problem. Its vulnerability intelligence covers traditional IT systems as well as cloud, IoT, operational technology, open source software. and third-party libraries.

    The company says it also tracks more than 105,000 vulnerabilities that aren't represented in CVE or the National Vulnerability Database, expanding the pool of flaws that security teams may need to evaluate.

    The cybersecurity tech giant's patented methodology profiles vulnerabilities using more than 60 technical characteristics, including whether a flaw can be exploited remotely without authentication, whether it affects operational technology systems, and how exploitation could affect data availability.

    Those characteristics form a multi-factor fingerprint. The model maps each vulnerability against clusters containing flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks and assigns a Low, Medium, High, or Critical Ransomware Risk rating.

    Sources indicate that flashpoint says the rating can be generated when a vulnerability is disclosed, rather than requiring security teams to wait for public evidence of active exploitation. Ratings are then updated as new ransomware activity and threat intelligence emerge.

    Within Flashpoint Ignite, Ransomware Risk appears alongside CVSS, EPSS, Social Risk, and exploit maturity. The idea isn't to replace existing scoring systems, but to give administrators additional information when deciding what to remediate first.

    Nor does a High or Critical Ransomware Risk rating mean a vulnerability will necessarily be exploited. The model measures how closely its characteristics resemble vulnerabilities historically associated with ransomware attacks.

    According to recent reports, for security teams facing thousands of potential vulnerabilities, that distinction matters. The flaw carrying the highest severity score isn't necessarily the one that most closely resembles what ransomware operators have historically chosen to attack.

    "Despite being the most popular indicator for priority, we know that severity alone doesn't tell you whether a vulnerability will be exploited or used in ransomware," stated Ben Haynes, Data Science & Analytics Lead at Flashpoint and co-inventor of the patented methodology.

    "A vulnerability can score low on a traditional severity scale and still share the characteristics we repeatedly see in ransomware attacks.".

    For more information, go to the Flashpoint site.
